data.title: The miraculous rain that saved a Roman army by the Hron
data.excerpt: The territory of present-day Slovakia first came directly into the centre of world events under the emperor Marcus Aurelius (161 – 180), when his troops pushed deep into the valleys of the Váh, the Nitra and the Hron during the Marcomannic Wars. In 172 a Roman unit surrounded by the Quadi by the Hron was saved by a sudden downpour, an episode recorded by the historian Cassius Dio.
data.metaTitle: The miraculous rain that saved the Romans
data.metaDescription: Marcus Aurelius and the Marcomannic Wars in present-day Slovakia: the story of the miraculous rain that, according to the sources, saved the Roman troops.

timeline.title: The Marcomannic Wars begin
timeline.description: The Marcomanni, the Quadi and the Iazyges attacked the Roman Empire, beginning the Marcomannic Wars, which lasted almost two decades.

timeline.title: Roman campaigns in the territory of present-day Slovakia
timeline.description: Marcus Aurelius attacked the territory of the Germanic peoples; his troops penetrated into the valleys of the Váh, the Nitra and the Hron.

timeline.title: The miraculous rain by the Hron
timeline.description: A Roman unit surrounded by the Quadi by the Hron was saved by a sudden rain and hailstorm, which contemporaries ascribed to the intervention of the gods.

timeline.title: The campaigns continue
timeline.description: Marcus Aurelius continued with a further campaign against the Germanic tribes.

children.text: The territory of present-day Slovakia first came directly into the centre of world events during the reign of the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius (161 – 180). In 161 the Germanic Marcomanni and Quadi, together with the Sarmatian Iazyges, who lived as nomads between the Danube and the Tisza, attacked the territory of the Roman Empire, thereby beginning the so-called Marcomannic Wars, which lasted two decades. Marcus Aurelius first drove them out of his own territory and then – in 172 – 175 and 177 – 180 – attacked their territory, his troops penetrating deep into the valleys of the rivers Váh, Nitra and Hron. In 172 a curious event took place by the Hron. In the course of a hot summer day a Roman unit found itself surrounded and was threatened with death by thirst. It was saved, however, by a sudden and unexpected rain, in which all those present saw the intervention of the gods. The story is recorded by the historian Cassius Dio (around 155 – after 235) in his Roman History.

blocks.text:
Indeed, after many hard struggles and dangers Marcus Aurelius subdued the Marcomanni and the Iazyges. And against the so-called Quadi there arose from this a great war, and an incredible victory fell to his lot: or rather, it was a gift from a god. For when the Romans found themselves in a perilous position in the battle, the divine power saved them in an incredible manner. For when the Quadi had surrounded them in a convenient place, the Romans fought bravely with their shields pressed together. Then the barbarians broke off the fight, expecting that they would easily take them captive once they were exhausted by the burning heat and by thirst. They blocked off everything round about, so that the Romans could obtain water from nowhere; for they also far outnumbered them. So when the Romans found themselves in the utmost straits, being exhausted and covered with wounds, exposed to the scorching sun and to thirst, and when for this reason they were no longer able either to fight or to withdraw anywhere, but remained standing drawn up in formation on the spot, burnt by the heat, suddenly a mass of clouds gathered and a heavy downpour came down, which certainly happened by divine intervention. For it is related that a certain Egyptian mage, Arnuphis, whom Marcus Aurelius had with him, summoned by certain spells certain daemons and, among others, above all Hermes, the lord of the air. By their agency he is said to have drawn the rain down to the earth.
When the rain came down, at first they all lifted their faces to the sky and caught the water in their mouths. Then some held out their shields, others even their helmets, and drank greedily themselves and gave their horses to drink as well. And although the barbarians ran up to them, they did not stop drinking and at the same time strove to fight. Indeed some of them, even wounded, gulped down at once the water and the blood that ran down into their helmets. And they might perhaps have suffered a terrible disaster, because the enemy were pressing hard upon them while they were for the most part occupied with drinking, had not a mighty hailstorm with a multitude of lightning bolts broken out against the enemy. Then water and fire could be seen falling from the sky onto the same spot. Thus some were drenched and drank, while others were consumed by the fire and died. And the fire did not even touch the Romans, and if it did reach them anywhere it was at once extinguished, while the rain brought the barbarians no benefit at all, but like oil kindled the flames upon them even more, so that, drenched by the rain, they sought – water. Then some wounded themselves in order to put out the fire even with their own blood, while others fled even to the Romans, for they alone, it was said, had the saving water. And Marcus Aurelius himself, of course, had pity on them.
